title: An Ethics-Informed Online Mindfulness Program for Hospital Practitioners
official: ETHOS: A Modular Ethics-Informed Online Mindfulness Program for Emotional Well-Being, Moral Resilience and Burnout Prevention in Hospital Practitioners: A Mixed-Methods Single-Arm Proof-of-Concept Study
summary:
This study tests ETHOS, an online mindfulness program for hospital practitioners. ETHOS combines mindfulness training with a short reflection on morally difficult situations at work.

The main questions are:

* Do enough practitioners enroll and stay in the study?
* Do participants complete the modules and practice between sessions?
* Are participants satisfied with the program?

The study also describes changes in emotional exhaustion, well-being, stress and moral distress over 18 weeks. This first study is not designed to show whether the program works.

About 30 practitioners from one hospital in France will take part. Adult practitioners involved in patient care can take part, for example physicians, nurses and allied health professionals. All participants will receive the program. There is no comparison group.

Participants will:

* Follow one online module each week for six weeks (about one hour per week)
* Follow a booster module at week 10
* Be invited to do a guided practice of 5 or 10 minutes each day
* Fill in questionnaires before the program and at weeks 6, 10 and 18

Researchers will also interview 10 to 12 participants about their experience of the program.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Hospital practitioner (for example physician, resident, nurse or allied health professional) currently employed at the study hospital and involved in patient care
* Aged 18 years or older
* Able to provide informed consent
* Able to access the online platform (internet-enabled computer or smartphone)
* Willing and able to complete at least four of the six weekly modules during the six-week delivery window

Exclusion Criteria:

* Current severe psychiatric episode requiring acute treatment (for example active psychosis, or severe major depression with high suicide risk)
* Current substance dependence
* Any condition that would make participation in mindfulness practice unsafe or impractical, as judged by the participant and, if needed, their treating clinician
